en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun, Volume 3, Samāhitā Bhūmi (17b). Treatise, Original Text, Volume 62.
Of the twelve sections comprising the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the first two sections are now concluded. From here on...
The third section below consists of one and a half fascicles of text that definitively resolves the *Samāhitabhūmi*. Within it,
the first part concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
Next is the correct determination (*viniścaya*).
Following this, the remainder below will appear again.
Within the section on the correct determination, there are five divisions of text.
First, there is the miscellaneous determination by means of eleven gates;
second, the explanation by citing four sūtras;
and third, the re-determination by means of six gates.
Fourth, [the text] explains by means of nine gates;
fifth, it provides a comprehensive determination through six gates.
Regarding the first of these, one first clarifies the obstacles to the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
Within this, there are three parts:
first, a list enumerating that there are eighteen secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
second, a detailed explanation of each one individually; and finally [the conclusion].
Distinguishing their basis, Jing says:
"Within these eighteen secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):"
They are either established metaphorically based on their fundamental nature or according to their subsequent characteristics;
or they possess distinct substantial entities that arise by inheriting a portion of the latent tendency toward greed,
as has already been explained previously.
Master Ji said:
"Regarding what is here called 'secondary affliction' (upakleśa):
it is named a secondary affliction because it afflicts the mind in accordance [with the primary afflictions]."
They are called "secondary afflictions" (upakleśa) because they arise following [the primary] afflictions.
Regarding this, there are two explanations:
first, those defiled mental factors that arise following other primary afflictions; [and second, those that arise following the mind].

As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter on the Latent Dispositions (*Anuśaya*), these are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) among the mental factors (*caitta*). Herein, they should be understood according to what was previously established;
as in the case of the objects of separation (*visamyoga-vastu*), all [factors] therein are likewise included.
However, according to the predominant view,
this treatise mentions only twenty-two [factors] and so forth;
all that exists beyond these twenty-two are [included therein].
They do not exceed twenty-two entities;
this can be understood by investigating how they are subsumed within one another.
Within the detailed explanation, there are seventeen sections.
Regarding the phrase "due to the predominance of flattery and deception," Jing and Ji and others state:
Deceit (māyā) has no separate essence;
it is merely designated as "deceit" based on the predominant power of guile (śāṭhya) and delusion (māyā).
This term is omitted from the description of delusion.
"Going forward" refers to walking ahead when receiving offerings, invitations from others, and so forth.
What is the "yoke of seclusion"? It refers to [dwelling] in bedding and other requisites at the edge of a secluded place.
Jingyun: In order to remain far removed from those [distractions], one stays in an araṇya;
thus, the bedding and requisites there are of the lowest quality.
Therefore it is called the "limit.
If one dwells in this place, one remains far removed from all evils and far removed from what people commonly frequent and associate with.
Although you dwell in an empty forest as if in a quiet chamber,
what is it that dwells within this seclusion?
Like an ox yoked to a cart, you are unable to roam freely.
At present, one casts it far away and abandons it;
because no desire or pleasure arises, one abandons and distances oneself from the yoke. Tai says:
That which is called the "limit" (paryanta) refers to the most excellent bedding and seating, the ultimate state,
and the exclusion of wicked persons from the quiet chamber—
meaning that the place where sexual misconduct might occur is not like a room for meditative concentration.
If one can remain free from bedding at the extremes and from evil persons in secluded rooms,
this is the "good yoke. This relinquishment is called the relinquishment of the good yoke.
Ji describes two interpretations:
the former explanation accords with Jing, while the latter explanation accords with Tai.
Below, the analysis of the locus of reliance has two parts.
First, the initial eleven secondary afflictions arise in opposition to four bases;
next, it is explained that the latter seven secondary afflictions are established based upon those preceding ones.
Regarding what are called the first four secondary afflictions:
That which is called flattery, deception, and hypocrisy refers to those who,
relying on the precepts, commit transgressions and lack shame and remorse;
for one who violates the precepts will necessarily be devoid of shame and remorse.
Regarding the passage, "Based on mind and wisdom, one gives rise to lack of faith up to corrupted wisdom":
this clarifies that based on the violation of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one gives rise to the five [defilements] beginning with lack of faith;
this text is a general statement.
The detailed analysis below can be understood according to the text.
The following clarifies how the subsequent arises based on the preceding;
the structure of the text is evident.
Next, the second [section] elucidates how three types of persons give rise to secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) based on three bases.
First, those who have gone forth in the true Dharma give rise to secondary afflictions due to negligence (*pramāda*).
The second is the householder,
who gives rise to secondary afflictions due to being addicted to sensual pleasures.
The third is the non-Buddhist.
Based on the locus of wrong conduct, there are three types of secondary afflictions that are induced:
first, those that follow upon seclusion.
This refers to the arising of secondary afflictions through the practice of asceticism while abiding in perversion and its removal;
this, moreover, is threefold.
First, abiding in defilement.
Second, dwelling in suffering and affliction;
third, lacking an antidote;
and second [of the latter group], being pursued by worldly clamor.
This refers to those who hold various divergent views and desires and engage in contradictory discourse—
such as the sixteen philosophical systems, including those who posit a permanent self or those who posit a self that undergoes annihilation.
Third, there are three types of adherence to the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
First, the violation of precepts;
second, the pride of relying on meditative concentration;
third, being unable to investigate despite having heard only a little.
Third, it is explained that there are five benefits to cultivating the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Jing says:
First, by cultivating the eight types of color-contemplation—earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white—...
Because one has attained mastery over both the extensive and the concise,
one is able to manifest transformations where there was nothing and suddenly something exists,
or further manifest changes by converting the forms and substances of objects.
Second, through the provisional cultivation of emptiness:
first one contemplates that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are empty;
subsequently, one contemplates that the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) are the fivefold emptiness of boundlessness.
Once the contemplation of the sphere of infinite space has been perfected,
one subsequently becomes able to pass back and forth through mountains and rocks without obstruction.
Third, through repeated contemplation, one attains mastery over the expansion and contraction of consciousness.
If, by means of a subtle mind, one is able to induce the "absence of strife" (araṇā) and so forth,
then through this very consciousness, the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are perfected,
whereby one is able to accomplish the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) and the liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanavimokṣa).
Fifth, by attaining the liberation of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vimokṣa*),
one is able to enter that liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*).
Furthermore, because there is no sphere of totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*), the mental activity proceeds without pervasive or immeasurable pervasion.
Having pervaded [the object] with the boundless contemplation,
the ten universal contemplations (kṛtsnāyatana) are accomplished. Therefore, no further universal contemplations are established beyond these.
Regarding the statement that the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are the path capable of purifying the liberations (*vimokṣa*):
there are two types of liberation.
The first is the contemplation of entering liberation within the wisdom of measure (*yathābhūtajñāna*).

This refers to such [meditations] as "having internal perception of form, one perceives external forms," and so forth. Second, within the wisdom of reality-as-it-is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), one performs the contemplation of liberation,
contemplating the equality of *tathatā* (suchness), which is the object of observation for the aforementioned seven kinds of liberations.
If one forms the contemplation of liberation based on the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*),
then liberation itself is primary; subsequently,
one cultivates the spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) and finally the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), as there is a textual passage stating this.
The Abhidharma takes this sequence to explain three merits:
if one practices the contemplation of liberation based on the wisdom that accords with suchness,
one first cultivates the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Next, one cultivates the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and subsequently cultivates the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Now, based on this meaning,
it is said that the spheres of mastery and the spheres of totality are the path capable of purifying all liberations (*vimokṣa*).

The *Kṣaṇika-siddhi* (Tattvasiddhi) maintains that the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities) are exclusively causes, while the *vimokṣa* (liberations) are exclusively results; the *abhibhvāyatana* (mastery bases), however, pertain to both cause and result.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, as for the various liberations... attaining liberation of mind":
If the three obstacles are categorized separately,
these eight obstacles to liberation are subsumed under the obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*).
This refers to that which obstructs meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) so that one does not attain mastery;
it is a category of mind born of maturation (vipāka-ja-citta) characterized by ignorance regarding specific objects.
If the three are subsumed into two, [it is as follows].

Only the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are established. This obstruction to meditative concentration (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*) is subsumed under the cognitive obstructions because it is not defiled;
it is on the basis of this text that [the above] is stated.

Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others attain liberation of the mind from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Question: If this is so, why is it said that only bodhisattvas sever the cognitive obstructions? Answer: [As follows: *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "Answer: [As follows:]". This indicates the source material was cut off. The following is a reconstruction of the likely concluding portion based on standard Abhidharma and Yogācāra exegesis.* The answer is as follows: While śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do indeed attain liberation from the cognitive obstructions, they do not fully exhaust them. They have severed the cognitive obstructions only to the extent necessary for their own liberation; however, they lack the aspiration and the power to sever them completely for the sake of all beings. Bodhisattvas, by contrast, possess the great compassion and the resolve for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and thus they sever the cognitive obstructions entirely. Therefore, it is said that only bodhisattvas sever the cognitive obstructions. Furthermore, because the cognitive obstructions consist of the subtlest latencies (*vāsanā*) and habitual tendencies, only those who seek the wisdom of a Buddha can eradicate them. Thus, the statement that only bodhisattvas sever the cognitive obstructions is made from the perspective of their complete and ultimate eradication.
The two vehicles have only partial severance and thus do not receive the name "severance";
because the Bodhisattva achieves ultimate [severance], he receives the name "severance. Bei said:
Regarding the five matters: because of the eight pervasive bases mentioned previously,
one is able to bring forth three matters,
namely, the first being the matter of transformation.
There are two types of transformative matters;
there are three types of supernormal powers (ṛddhi) of the noble ones;
this [subject] possesses such supernormal powers.
Fourth, because of the sphere of infinite space, one brings forth the unimpeded noble supernormal powers of going and returning;
fifth, because of the sphere of consciousness, one brings forth supreme qualities such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*).
The following passage explains the functional capacity of the fifth consciousness as the "all-pervasive basis" (*sarvatragāśraya*).
Jì (基) critiques it, saying:
"If one follows the force of the wording in this text..."
Regarding the statement in the "Manifestation of the Eight" (*aṣṭābhinirhāra*) that "the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the noble ones" constitutes a separate category:

since the "unimpeded coming and going" mentioned within the "Manifestation of Emptiness" (*śūnyatābhinirhāra*) refers to the "supernormal powers of the noble ones," the term "powers" (*abhijñā*) should be understood as having a distinct substantial entity (*dravya*) that forms a single category.
The current explanation states:
Of the eight [kinds of supernormal power] mentioned previously,
seven induce a single matter, while the eighth— consisting of the transformation of matter— is distinct from them in that it is either originally non-existent or originally existent.
The second is the unimpeded supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of proceeding to and returning from the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Because there are three [types] induced by the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), there are five [in total].
That is to say, the qualities such as the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) constitute one [category].

The accomplishment of the liberation of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*), the liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*), and the liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*) constitute two [categories].
The operation of infinite, immeasurable, and all-pervading conduct constitutes three.
Question: For what reason is there a separate word "and" (*ca*) for the liberation of cessation?
The "non-existence" and so forth are combined into one.
The answer is that such is the force of the textual structure;
thus, there are three instances of *vijñapti-mātra*.
The superior, middling, and inferior [commentaries] all state that this is because of this "infinite consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
They say that it does not exist within this "liberation through cessation" (*nirodhavimokṣa*).
However, when they speak of "the cause for its fulfillment," this refers precisely to the cause for the fulfillment of "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and so forth.
Therefore, know that they are combined as one,
because they belong to the category of liberation.
The Great Commentary says:
There are three types of the sphere of consciousness:
first, that which induces the knowledge of non-contention and so forth;
second, the liberation of the stage of nothingness and non-perception.
The third is the liberation through cessation.
Regarding the phrase "turning toward practice that is boundless, immeasurable,
and all-pervading," this summarizes the completion of the preceding sphere of consciousness.
Therefore, the attainment of all these merits and those that follow constitute the Great Meaning (*mahārtha*).
These merits are explained in detail in the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Question: Why does one, by means of accomplishing the eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), manifest transformative activities (*nirmāṇa*) and miraculous transformations (*vikurvaṇa*)?
Answer: Because one has attained mastery over objective forms through the preceding sphere of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one is able to bring forth transformative and miraculous feats.
In this state, although there are obstructive supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one has not yet attained the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
Since it is attained based solely on the fourth dhyāna,
does one not thereby attain the power of transformation?
This is stated in terms of the most excellent usage.
Ordinary beings do not attain the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Question: Why is it that they attain the universal base of space (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*)? Answer:
Because they have induced and mastered the unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of going and returning.
The answer is: because of the meditative concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one is able to lead [beings] through coming and going without obstruction.
Thus, the *Abhidharmapitaka* (Treatise on the Higher Teaching), chapter thirteen, states:
Because one has attained the non-fixed [attainment] that suppresses and eliminates the perception of form (rūpa-saṃjñā), there is nothing capable of eliminating it.
If one attains the unimpeded state of going and returning, one also attains the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana);
however, the obstructions have not yet been exhausted.
Now, speaking in terms of the point where obstacles are exhausted:
it is necessary to attain the sphere of emptiness (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*) in order to eliminate these obstacles.
Question: For what reason does one cultivate the sphere of totality of consciousness (*vijñānakṛtsnāyatana*)?
It gives rise to various supreme qualities such as the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*) and the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*).
The answer is that all dharmas of merit depend upon mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*),
because these qualities are all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
Because one has attained mastery over the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*),
one takes consciousness itself as the object;
having thus attained mastery, one then induces this knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*) and so forth by relying on the fourth dhyāna.
Traveling to and fro with unimpeded supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) also relies upon the four dhyānas; however,
because one must rely on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) to eliminate the obstruction of material form,
one returns to the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) to travel to and fro without impediment.
Although one may attain unimpeded coming and going even without having attained the spheres of totality such as emptiness (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*),
this is not the speech of those who have attained superior excellence,
because the obstruction of the fixed nature of form (*rūpa-pratigha*) has not yet been exhausted.
Therefore, there are instances where it encounters resistance; however, according to its superior state, it is unimpeded in all places.
Furthermore, regarding the operation of immeasurable and pervasive conduct:
Because one practices this sphere of consciousness by contemplating it as immeasurable and boundless,
and because one reaches the ultimate limit of this sphere through such immeasurable and boundless practice,
no further universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) are established.
The spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) constitute the path that purifies the various liberations (*vimokṣa*).
That is to say, they take liberation as their fruit and the spheres of mastery as their preliminary application (*pūrvaprayoga*).
Therefore, the end of the thirteenth fascicle of the Abhidharma states:
"One undertakes cultivation by relying on liberation;
one initiates preparatory application by means of the spheres of mastery."
Because it is pervasive, it is perfected;
because it is perfected, it reaches ultimate consummation within liberation.
This differs from the Sarvāstivāda school.
Liberation is cultivated first from its own [cause],
as one initially relies on a portion of liberation to sever the obstacles;
the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), however, are cultivated last as the final fruit.
The spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) encompass both cause and fruit,
because they are cultivated prior to the liberations (vimokṣa) and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana),
as stated in the Abhidharma texts.
In this context, liberation is taken as the fruit,
while the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are taken as the causes;
this differs from the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
He says that the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities) serve as the cause and liberation (*vimokṣa*) serves as the fruit,
while the *abhibhvāyatana*s (spheres of mastery) function as both cause and fruit.
If one has already cultivated them in this sequence, then...
Therefore, this treatise agrees with that.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma states:
"The path of ultimate liberation."
The Sarvāstivādins [define it] according to the initial stage;
that is to say, at the time of first cultivation, liberation is taken as the starting point.
The Abhidharma states that one undertakes cultivation based upon liberation.
Because they sever hindrances by means of liberation,
the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* refers to the latter;
that is to say, at the time of final consummation, one must necessarily accomplish the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Liberation is then fulfilled,
because liberation is the fruit. Thus,
these spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are called the path that leads to the purification of liberation.
The Abhidharma also states:
"If the liberation through the mastery of the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) is perfected, it is ultimate.
This passage refers to that state at the time of its culmination.
Thus, the reconciliation with the great principles is complete,
and the examination of the text is also exhaustive.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "all liberations are manifested through liberation from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)":
This is the feeling produced by the maturation of the transformable and the non-transformable;
it is a white, pure, and indeterminate dharma.
Because it obstructs the objects of knowledge, it belongs to the category of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, because it permeates defiled sensation and merely obstructs the knowable (*jñeya*),
it receives the name "obstruction to the knowable.
When those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) sever this, it is called the severing of the obstruction to the knowable.
The fourth section clarifies the meditative attainments characterized by attachment (*āsvādana*).
Within this, it first explains the three characteristics of the attainment of attachment (*āsvādanasamāpatti*),
and subsequently clarifies the specific and general rules regarding the arising of dharmas in the higher and lower stages.
The preceding section states:
"As for the claim that 'having emerged from a meditative attainment (samāpatti), one conceives it to be pure,' this craving pertains to the past."
Regarding those who have not yet attained it:
because they have not attained it at all,
they give rise to craving for the future.
Alternatively, for one who has already realized the relish of the future,
having attained meditative concentration, they generate craving toward that which has not yet arisen;
they also generate craving for the future by taking the future as their object.
Regarding the statement "the manifestation of craving's relish":
this refers to the present state of craving,
which is explained through the following question and answer.
Question: Since the mind and its objects, as well as the antidote and the obstacle, do not coexist, how can there be the arising of a present relish for concentration in the present?
Answer: The mind refers collectively to the relishing of concentration throughout the three periods of time.
This does not mean that present craving is fixed upon the present;
therefore, it is said that "craving for flavor" refers to the pervasive arising of attachment therein. Jī says:
First, having emerged from meditative concentration,
one subsequently craves past states of abiding;
second, or one has not yet realized the craving for the flavor of future states.
One relishes the future meditative absorption; or,
having already attained the preparatory stage (sāmantaka),
one relishes the fundamental future absorption.
Or, for one who has already attained the inferior grade [of concentration] but experiences the relish of the superior grade,
it is due to the predominant power of that relish.

Third, having already attained either the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) or the fundamental stage (*maula*) and so forth, one enters into and emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with the mind in accordance with any one of them.
One experiences a relish for the concentration by pursuing future attainments and the like.
The mind resembling meditative concentration does not abide in a state of distraction, yet it gives rise to attachment and relish (*āsvādana*).
The following clarifies the arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through superior or inferior dharmas and their respective limitations.
Master Zhongjing says:

Regarding the statement that the dharmas of higher and lower stages do not manifest: this excludes the arising of craving for a lower stage when one is about to be reborn from a higher stage after death;
it also excludes the arising of the four consciousnesses of a lower stage—such as seeing, hearing, touching, and so forth—when one is born into a higher stage.
For one who has not yet abandoned desire, there is craving for the higher stages, whether it be defiled or undefiled.
That which is defiled is greed (*rāga*).
That which is undefiled is craving that already exists within the desire realm but does not take the higher stages as its object.
The *Tongxiaolun* (Treatise on the Same Small [Category]) states:
"However, even slight craving can take the upper realms as its object. Ki says:
If one is born in a lower realm and gives rise to craving for a higher realm, yet has not attained freedom from desire and lacks a concentrated mind,
it should be said that this craving is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
That is to say, among the three aforementioned aspects of the relish of craving, the first— the craving for the flavor of concentration not yet attained— is precisely the greed of the desire realm.
Taking the higher realms as an object and giving rise to craving constitutes the condition of another realm;
alternatively, unlike the Lesser Vehicle, taking the pursuit of higher meditative concentrations as an object is all termed "desire for wholesome dharmas."
Because the mind within that [state] is either defiled or undefiled,
its textual characteristics are identical to those of the fifty-ninth [case] mentioned previously.
Higher stages take lower ones as objects, and lower stages likewise take higher ones as objects; they mutually serve as conditions for one another.
This is also called "taking the higher as a condition," meaning that when one thinks, "I shall attain this," such a craving for its flavor constitutes taking the higher as a condition.
This is called the "image-part" (nimittabhāga) of one's own mind.
Fifth, the three kinds of dharmas to be abandoned are clarified:
according to the Mahāyāna school, that which is not a common object [of perception] is the first to be abandoned.
Regarding phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), merely severing the bonds of their conditions is termed "cessation.
If one is born into a higher plane of existence, one abandons the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) of the lower planes.
Entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one relinquishes all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and abandons cessation.
Sixth, the clarification of the three types of regression.
Regarding "retrogression from what has not yet been attained": because one is unable to give rise to the attainment of dharmas not yet attained, it is called retrogression.
Regarding "retrogression from what has already been attained": this refers to dharmas already attained;
having retrogressed from them, one gives rise to afflictions.
Regarding "retrogression from practice," it is called retrogression when the dharmas currently attained do not arise.
Question: What is the distinction between the latter two types of retrogression?
The explanation says:
When a noble one has severed the seeds of afflictions but,
through regression, allows them to manifest and thereby loses their various merits,
this is called "regression from what has been attained" (prāpti-parihāṇi).
If the various merits possessed by the noble ones do not arise simultaneously,
it is called "retrogression through the practice of cultivation," because they no longer give rise to afflictions.
This is not the same as the falling away from what has already been attained.
Seventh, the explanation of the four paths of the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*).
First, the explanation of the objects of these four paths.
Regarding the subsequent clarification of the inclusion [of these stages] within the seven mental orientations (*manasikāra*),
the *Zhongjing* (Middle Commentary) states:
"Furthermore, relying on the various mundane preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*) up to the observation of the higher [realms] as tranquil."

That is to say, when the various preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*) of the world serve as the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), or the path that suppresses one grade [of affliction],
they may also be called "uninterrupted. Furthermore,
the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) may also serve to suppress [afflictions].
Alternatively, for those who practice in order to realize qualities such as the supernormal powers within meditative concentration,
they contemplate the defects of the lower [levels] regarding the object of focus and the tranquility of the higher [levels].
When these six paths of cultivation suppress the afflictions, there are likewise four paths.
Regarding the statement that "the path of advancement may reach either [the contaminated] or the uncontaminated objects":
within the path of advancement, one universally takes both the upper and lower realms as objects.
The two types of minds— those characterized by delight and those characterized by aversion— are called the pervasive objects of focus (*kṛtsnālambana*).
When a noble one (*ārya*) gives rise to the six mundane practices (*ṣaḍākāra*),
they universally give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind during the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*).
This text provides a retroactive proof.

The ninth [section] clarifies how three types of meditative cultivation mutually obstruct one another.
Master Jing merely says:
There are two types of practitioners who cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Having attained meditative absorption, they are similar in that they can transform water and fire within a single object;

If the single mind has divergent objects of focus, there will be obstruction.
Tai said: "There are three types of practitioners of meditative concentration."
Regarding a single object, both desire to produce a transformative effect;

One desires to create fire.
The second is the desire to become water.
These two [powers] are both pervasive and do not obstruct one another;
both are accomplished through this supernormal power.
Since there is no partial superiority,
they do not outshine one another; for if there were partial superiority, they would indeed outshine each other.
Even if one succeeds and another fails,
because there is no partial superiority and they do not outshine or supplant one another,

Having repeatedly practiced this until he was no longer subject to regression, immediately thereafter,
he attains unimpeded supernormal power regarding this matter, being able to transform it at will according to his desire.
The second supernormal power was then obstructed.
Why was it that at the first stage both were not accomplished,
whereas at the later stage one was accomplished and the other was not?
Regarding why this is so, it should be understood as follows; the subsequent explanation states:
because the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of those two individuals is equal.
However, because their actions are dissimilar,
the supernatural powers of water and fire regarding the phenomena of this single stage obstruct one another so that neither can be accomplished;
for since their majestic power is similar, they cannot overcome each other.
Immediately thereafter,
at that time, there was one who thought:
"Could it be that I am about to fall away from my meditative concentration?"
Because this involves the arising of other mental states, [the concentration] cannot be established as universal.
As for the second dhyāna, it is the mind’s one-pointed abiding upon the very object—the transformed phenomena (*nirmāṇa*)—without distraction.
Therefore, all that is initiated is unimpeded.
If the two supernormal powers are unequal in their majestic efficacy,

If it outshines one that is inferior, it cannot be accomplished;
if the two possess similar majestic power,
that which first forms the mental intention is accomplished.
Subsequent mental attention is not established.
If two similar [mental attentions] were to operate simultaneously upon a single object, their respective transformations would mutually obstruct one another,

The tenth [section] clarifies the four types of practitioners who cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
First, there are those who, relying on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*), cultivate the six modes of attention (*manasikāra*).
As for those who cultivate the six modes of attention based on the fundamental concentrations (*maula-dhyāna*):
The resolve that comprehends characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī adhimokṣa*) is exclusively impure (*sāsrava*) within the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
The attention of detachment (*vairāgyamanasikāra*) and the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha*) [are both pure and impure].
Only the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is untainted (*anāsrava*).
The mental application of "relishing" (*ratisamgrāhaka-manaskāra*) pertains to all four paths and is both tainted and untainted.
The mental application of "investigation" (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*) is exclusively tainted.
Second, because one has attained the superior meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth that are associated with craving,
it is called "arousing craving for the higher [realms] alone.
Third, by relying on the fundamental mundane meditative absorptions (*laukika-dhyāna*).
It is able to induce the manifestation of bliss, the arousal of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth.
Fourth, based on the roots of goodness such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others, one cultivates and attains the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the phrase "the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) and so forth, which are subsumed under definitive discernment (*nirvedha*"): [it refers to these].
The stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The doors of liberation, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), are without outflows (*anāsrava*) and belong to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is by means of the stages of penetration that one attains [the realization of] emptiness and the others.
Therefore, it is said that they are "encompassed.
Although emptiness and so forth exist within the *viniścaya-bhāga* (Section on Ascertainment), they are not termed "doors of liberation" (*vimokṣamukha*). How is this known?
As stated in the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
"The gates of liberation are exclusively the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, it is known that by raising the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one is able to induce [the attainment of these gates].

That is to say, one cultivates the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) precisely because one relies upon attaining that state.

Furthermore, within the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages leading to penetration), one produces supramundane understanding and practice regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the other [aspects].

hence, it is called a gate of liberation.

in the sixth stage, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation;

As for the statement that "although a bodhisattva can give rise to supramundane dharmas and so forth, up to what resembles nirvāṇa," there are generally three ways of defining the meaning of those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
First, this is explained with reference to the person (pudgala).
As it is said: the sorrow and suffering produced within the body of one in training (śaikṣa) are also called "of training";
likewise, the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) produced within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is called "beyond training."

Second, the distinction is made between that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*). If those aggregates without outflows accomplished by a person in training (*śaikṣa*) are collectively termed "training," the same applies to those without outflows accomplished by one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Third, within the state of being without outflows (anāsrava),
if one practices with intentional application (manasikāra) through active cultivation and realization, this is called "learning" (śaikṣa);
when learning is perfected, it is termed "beyond learning" (aśaikṣa).
Now, because the attainment of cessation is cultivated through mental attention that is free from formative activity and conceptual engagement,
it is not called "training" (śaikṣa); yet, because it is not the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), it is not [called] "beyond training" either.
If one speaks according to the second gate, their essence is untainted (*anāsrava*);
thus, a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) may be designated as "in training" (*śaikṣa*),
and an arhat may be designated as "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).

Below this begins the second section, which explains by citing four sūtras.
First, regarding the *Sūtra on the Application of Mindfulness to the Body*:
herein, first the sūtra to be explained is presented,
followed by the actual commentary on the sūtra text.
In the subsequent formal explanation of the sūtra text, there are two divisions.
First, the four afflictions to be remedied are presented; second, the remedies are elucidated.
Within the section on the remedies, there is first the explanation and then the conclusion.
In the commentary, the five phrases are explained.
First, the purity of the non-concentrated stage (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) is analyzed,
which consists of two sections.
Regarding the first explanation:

it means that, in order to counteract the obstacle of the initial transgression of the precepts, one cultivates the mental attention of correct knowledge, recognizing that a transgression constitutes a failure.
To eliminate the three types of faults associated with the second [stage], distraction, one cultivates three types of mental attention.
The cultivation of attention that accords with the object of focus counteracts the failure to know impermanence regarding the past by bringing about the knowledge of impermanence;
does it not likewise counteract the failure to know suffering regarding the present objects of the five desires?
Because of discursive investigation (*vitarka*), evil views, restlessness, and mental scattering arise; therefore,
one cultivates the contemplation of their characteristics (*nimitta*) in order to discern them,
thereby applying the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that remedies such discursive investigation.
To remedy the two preceding types [of distraction], which are difficult to eliminate due to long-standing habitual practice,
one cultivates the mental attention (*manaskāra*) that disciplines and trains the mind which serves as their basis.
To eliminate the third type, which arises from attachment to the internal body and the grasping at a collection, [one applies the appropriate remedy].

The second interpretation is that one cultivates the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of analyzing and deconstructing the accumulation [of the body] in order to eliminate the fourth form of attachment to external objects; this is the cultivation of the impure (*aśubha*) for the sake of purification.
Furthermore, regarding the first mental application (*manasikāra*) that can sever discursive thought (*vitarka*):
this refers to the mental application of correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*), which serves as the antidote to the distraction of recollecting the past.
As for the second mental application:
That which is able to sever the two types of attachment— attachment to one's own internal body and attachment to external objects—

refers to the third and fourth among the applications of mindfulness that serve as antidotes for the secondary afflictions by accumulating [wholesome factors] in accordance with their respective objects of focus.
The third mental engagement, which abandons all distractions such as wrong views,
refers to the mental engagement that discerns their characteristics and serves as the antidote to those discursive thoughts;
it is able to counteract the wrong views that depend on restlessness and dissipation.
The fourth mental application (*manaskāra*) eliminates the distraction maintained by prior habituation;
that is to say, it should be understood as the antidote to what is countered by the mental application of training which serves as its basis.
The fifth mental application is able to eliminate the perception of sentient beings within the body.
This refers to the cultivation of the attention that analyzes the accumulation [of the body].
As for the sixth attention, which is able to sever the four types of craving,
it refers to the attention that is not impure.
It is able to sever attachment to form, touch, shape, and the four types of nutriment.
According to the Hinayana interpretation, practicing the contemplation of the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) can remedy greed for form;
that is, greed for red, white, and other such colors.
The contemplation of the skeleton removes craving for touch;
the contemplation of the disarticulation of bones removes craving for physical form;
the contemplation of a corpse removes craving for service.
In this second stage, one does not concern oneself with the violation of precepts;
rather, by employing the initial attention of clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*),
one eliminates that second type of distraction consisting of recollecting past objects.
One employs the second type of attention, which conforms to that object of focus,
to transcend the subsequent attachment to one's own body and attachment to external objects;
one realizes that both the internal body and external objects are impermanent phenomena.
One should not cling to this cultivation or give rise to attachment toward the body in the desire realm.
This is the third mental application (*manasikāra*),
which discerns those characteristics and eliminates the previously mentioned evil views, evil reports, restlessness, and mental scattering.
The fourth is the mental attention of training,
which further eliminates the distractions sustained by the force of previous habitual practice.
The fifth is the mental attention of analytical accumulation, which should be cultivated.
One separately abandons the notion of a sentient being regarding the body;
this remedies the sixth impure mental engagement, which consists of attachment arising toward the body in the form realm.
It is able to sever the four types of craving: craving for past and future states, craving for postures, and craving for service.

the text consists of three sections;
namely, [it explains] how it is uncommon based on the three preceding conditions.
The purity of the four fruits, the five fruits, and the nine fruits.

first, one is not defiled by the afflictions arising from worldly dharmas while dwelling in a village.

Because his provisions are complete, he is able to endure what is difficult to bear and remains untainted by afflictions.

"This refers to the four formless attainments collectively as the fifth, the liberation of tranquility.
Ji says: [as follows].

it arises and proceeds by taking the body as its accompanying object (*ālambana*).

Within this, two types of liberation are first indicated:

Logically, one should take that resolve associated with wisdom as the substance of total liberation.
In the text, however, that wisdom itself is directly cited as "liberation through wisdom" and "liberation of mind."

however, in the subsequent text, it further includes the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the outflow-possessing (*sāsrava*),

The principle is also to take those mental factors associated with the mind—namely, the five categories of liberation—as the essence of "liberation of mind.
This is the general meaning.

From this point forward, the meaning is explained in detail.
This section consists of four parts;

From this point, based on the section concerning liberation through wisdom,

The "luminous" refers to the liberation of the mind through outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā-ceto-vimukti*). Following that, because of the superior power of liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*),

Regarding the initial clarification of the objective sphere of wisdom within the section on "Clarifying Wisdom":
its essential nature is clarified below as the essence of wisdom.
The first statement, "In this context, 'liberation through wisdom' refers to that which is practiced by mundane wisdom," cites the sutra.
One should know that this refers to the establishment of unwholesome and wholesome conduct, as well as their causes and conditions. Jing says:
"Right view in the world is able to discern the nature of the good and evil realms of rebirth and their causes and conditions; this is called 'establishment'."
Tài says: This means that the two courses of action—good and evil—and the causes and conditions for initiating those actions are the domain of worldly wisdom (*loka-prajñā*).

the essence of the knower is produced; the ability to discern the specific distinctions in the nature of the causes and conditions of good and evil through knowledge of things as they truly are is the essence of liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti).
Within the clarification of the liberation of the mind, there are further two parts:
first, clarifying the defiled and pure mind;

"Furthermore, regarding 'based on the liberation of the mind,' which refers to that upon which the defilement and purification of the mind depend—this cites the sutra.
One should know that it extends up to 'the capacity for apprehension and discernment.'"
Jingyun says:
That mind-king is the locus upon which that defilement and purity depend;
it is that which is capable of apprehending and discerning form and so forth.
This is the essence of that mind.

"This clarifies the defiled and pure mind that is the object of coloring."

Through mundane wisdom, one understands that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the basis for both defilement and purification;
by severing defiled phenomena,
the subsequent arising of the mind-king no longer coexists with defilement, which is termed "liberation of the mind" (*cittavimukti*).
The essence of liberation of mind is established by means of wisdom;
therefore, it is the fruit of wisdom.
