Regarding the explanation of how the liberation of the mind is liberated:
it should be understood that this means the mind emerges from its corresponding, associated, and subordinate categories of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).
That is to say, the pure mind is called "liberation of the mind" because it emerges from among these corresponding, associated, and subordinate categories of affliction.
The mind becomes defiled precisely through the power of wisdom,
as stated in the Sixty-fourth [Fascicle]:
"Regarding the hindrance of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa), it is said that because of it, the mind liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) attains liberation."
Regarding the hindrance to meditative concentration (*samādhy-āvaraṇa*): it is because of this that it is said the minds of all Tathāgatas are liberated.
That aforementioned hindrance to concentration is the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because the Tathāgata is free from these cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa), his mind attains liberation;
therefore, it is said that this is "liberation through wisdom" (prajñāvimukti) by the superior power [of that wisdom].
Master Ki further states:
Up to this point, by the predominant power of liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*), the fruit of the liberation of the mind (*ceto-vimukti*) is clarified.
That is to say, by virtue of the power of mundane wisdom (*loka-prajñā*) from previous lives,
the mind emerges from both the bondage of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) and the bondage of objects (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This means that "correspondence" (saṃprayoga) refers to the bond of perception (saṃjñā-bandhana),
while "intermingling" (saṃsṛṣṭa) refers to the bond of objective conditions (ālambana-bandhana).
Furthermore, "correspondence" refers to arising simultaneously or [in association].
The mixed [states] arise in alternation;
this is the fruit of mundane liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*).
It consists solely in the ability to remain untainted even when associated with or alternating with [defiled states].
It is not apart from the bonds of conditions and so forth;
if it were apart from them, it would be the fruit of the untainted liberation of mind (*anāsrava-citta-vimukti*).
Now, [I shall] explain.
Furthermore, because the defilements of the lower classes emerge, it is explained as the fruit of the liberation of the mind through clarity;
this differs from the textual judgments of the two previous masters.
However, since the specific scriptural version they relied upon has not been seen, it is impossible to know which is correct.
The following clarifies the two aspects within the liberation of the mind through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*):
first, the aspect of the object, and second, the aspect of the fruit.
Regarding the former, it says:
"By the superior power of liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*), it is that which is practiced by supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*). This is a citation of the scriptural text.
It should be understood that this refers to "that which reaches all objects."
Jingyun: Because of mundane wisdom and the liberation of the mind,
one is able to give rise to supramundane wisdom that comprehends all objects.
Tài says: "By virtue of the predominant power of mundane wisdom-liberation from previous lives, and that which is practiced by supramundane, untainted wisdom—
this is due to the predominant power of the two liberations of prior mind and wisdom."
Having realized that all objects are empty,
it next states that "the supramundane wisdom, the fruit of liberation of mind," and so forth;
this means that supramundane wisdom exhausts all defiled seeds.
Because it enables that mind to become ultimately free from defilement,
the mind is liberated;
furthermore, because it is the fruit of supramundane wisdom.
It is said that one should know this because it emerges from among all types of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).
Next, the characteristics of the fruit of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) will be explained in sequence.
This section contains two parts.
First, it clarifies mundane and supramundane wisdom, which, when summarized as one, is called right view.
Second, from "Furthermore, the supramundane... onwards, it specifically clarifies the characteristics of the fruit of supramundane right view.
Regarding this, Jing says:
"One should know that because it is eternally present before and after and has nothing with which to be contrasted" clarifies the True Suchness (tathatā) manifested by those two kinds of emptiness.
This is precisely the fruit realized through right view;
it is called "ordinary" before and "sage" after.
Although it passes through these temporal stages, its essence remains eternally unchanging.
The various paths of training arise because they depend on the presence of residual afflictions;
if that which is to be eliminated is absent, they cease and do not arise.
Depending upon their respective antidotes, some arise and others cease.
Therefore, it is called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).
This sentence establishes the thesis;
the following explanation has two parts.
This refers to the sequence of prior and subsequent.

When it says "if a phenomenon is that which is counteracted" or "if there is something produced that does not cease," this refers to the phenomena of the path of training; therefore, it says "if a phenomenon."
Because that which is to be countered exists, if the continuum of the untainted path of training is not extinguished,
it is said that "if that which is to be countered is not extinguished, there will be birth.
Alternatively, the severing of the seeds of evil is termed "that which is to be countered."
If, because one follows the outflows while training on the path,
the path of no-more-learning arises after those [outflows] have been extinguished, it is said that "birth exists.
Those dharmas are called "having a counterpart."
The fetters associated with that Truth of the Path are termed "with resistance" (sāpratigha).
Those that accord downwardly with suchness are "without resistance" (apratigha) dharmas.
Although there may be differences regarding liberation—such as being unarisen or not yet arisen—[they remain without resistance].
Furthermore, because that essence of *tathatā* is eternally existent, it is called "without opposition" (*apratigha*).
Moreover, regarding the phrase "even until this fruit is attained through purification," which cites the sūtra,
one should understand that it extends up to "and causes the faculties to become compliant with purification."
When the defiled mind has ceased and the pure mind arises, it does not become attached to objects and causes the retribution to accord with purity.
Master Ji says:
"This clarifies that because it is the fruit of right view, it is said to be permanent."
Regarding the phrase "if a phenomenon" (*yad dharmaḥ*), which serves to exclude conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) from the category of impermanence:
one interpretation states that "if a phenomenon" refers to all things collectively designated by the general term *dharma*.
If that which is to be remedied were to arise and not subsequently cease—
meaning, if the affliction to be remedied were to exist such that it does not cease along with the arising of the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga).
If that which is to be abandoned has not ceased while that which is to arise has already arisen—
meaning, if the afflictions to be abandoned have not ceased,
yet the path of uninterrupted transition and the afflictions have both ceased, and the path of liberation has already arisen.
Because these objects of abandonment and their antidotes involve cessation and arising,
one should know that they possess counterparts and are therefore impermanent. Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
If it is a phenomenon (*dharma*), it refers to the phenomena of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Regarding "if there is that which is to be remedied":

this means that from the stage prior to the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*) up until the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there may still be that which is to be remedied; thus, there is that which is to be remedied.
Prior to the vajra-mind, the paths and so forth are called "arisen and non-extinguished" because they arise repeatedly and are capable of arising in the present.
At the time of the subsequent vajra-mind, all afflictions are absent.
When that which is to be remedied by the name [of the path] is absent,
the previously attained path having ceased,
the subsequent path of the perfected fruit arises.
Therefore, it is said that after cessation there is arising.
Because this Truth of the Path possesses both arising and cessation, it is called impermanent;
because the unconditioned is not of this nature, it is permanent.
This merely excludes the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
If one does not interpret it as being prior to the generation of the vajra-mind (*vajracitta*),
then in the Mahāyāna, [the two truths] might not be understood as being simultaneous.
How can that which is to be remedied coexist with the path of non-arising and non-ceasing?
This subsequent explanation of the great meaning is identical to [the view of] Jing.
Second, the analysis of abiding.
Furthermore, regarding "the mind of liberation abides" up to "abiding through mutual connection":
for one whose mind is liberated, it is able to abide securely because life-force (*āyu*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) sustain one another in succession.

Third, in the section distinguishing the differences among the fruits, Master Jing supplements the text by stating: "Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the two kinds of fruits of liberation—mundane and supramundane"—this cites the Sūtra.
It should be understood that "until there is no further existence" means that if it is supramundane liberation, there is definitively no further existence;
if it is mundane liberation, its essence is still tainted (*sāsrava*).
If a person in training (śaikṣa) still possesses ignorance and craving, there will be future existence and rebirth;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), who lacks ignorance and craving, there is no future existence and no rebirth.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because they are mixed and associated," etc.:
That is to say, when that defiled mind is intermingled with and associated with various afflictions, it is not liberated.
When the defiled mind is severed and a pure mind arises, the mental factors upon which it depends also attain purification.
Therefore, that pure mind is not defiled by present conditions as it perceives its objects.
Jì (基) says:
"Regarding the phrase 'among all sensations and among causes and conditions'..."
Contact is the causal condition for feeling;
because it conditions the arising of craving, grasping, and so forth, there is subsequent birth.
As for the phrase "furthermore, because they are intermingled and associated," etc.:
This interpretation of the fruit of right view has no distinct meaning.

Regarding the statement in the fourth section on the differentiation of abidings— that which supplements the deficiency by saying "it is precisely the differentiation of the two abidings of liberation"—
one should know that this refers to the six types of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth.
The initial departure from lethargy and agitation constitutes one form of tranquility.
Regarding the statement, "because the purified consciousness sinks into equanimity," the term "sinks" (沒) is used metaphorically to describe meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
it does not mean that the consciousness actually ceases or literally sinks into a state of non-equanimity.
Regarding the statement that it is not "due to the equality of its basis":
because the mind is frequently agitated due to reliance on restlessness (*auddhatya*),
being free from that restlessness is now termed "relying on equality."
Second, it is called "entering tranquility" because one enters meditative absorption without relying on preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Third, it is called "emerging from tranquility" because one emerges from meditative absorption without relying on preparatory effort.
Fourth, while in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the three types of formations (*saṃskāra*) do not function; this is termed "tranquility."
5. Regarding "the mind is tranquil upon emerging from seclusion," the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called "emerging from seclusion" because the mind is constantly tranquil.
6. Regarding "because the mind is calm and still upon emerging from proximity,"...
Having completed the entry into and emergence from the meditative absorption of cessation through those three moments of mind,
these three moments of mind are called "proximate," because they are proximate to the meditative absorption of cessation.
First, the superior meditative concentrations of the form realm;
second, the superior meditative concentrations of the formless realm;
third, the supramundane untainted meditative concentrations.
Regarding the mind that enters and exits the formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*):
this refers to the mind that, having successively entered the formless absorptions, subsequently enters the form realm absorptions (*rūpa-dhyāna*).
Alternatively, it may also refer to the case where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, upon emerging from the absorption of cessation, immediately enter the form realm absorptions.
When emerging from the attainment of cessation and entering the formless attainments, one enters first the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
subsequently, one enters the sphere of nothingness,
or further back, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of infinite space.
If one emerges from the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and enters an untainted mind (anāsravacitta),
one enters into any one of the lower three formless attainments;
upon emerging from the attainment of cessation, one first gives rise to a formless concentration (ārūpyasamādhi).
Next, one arises in a dhyāna of the form realm;
or, emerging from the attainment of cessation, one enters an untainted (anāsrava) concentration.
These three types of mind arise only upon emerging from the attainment of cessation.
It is called "the mind becoming tranquil upon emerging from proximity.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that this consciousness is not only attained after emerging from the various meditative absorptions, but was also previously attained and arises as a present manifestation:
This statement that they are "previously obtained" is based on the fact that one has previously attained their respective categories;
however, there are also cases where they have not been previously attained and arise only upon emerging from meditative absorption.
Therefore, it is said that they are "also previously obtained."
Regarding the statement, "In this context, up to the last one, it is not by way of sequential meditative absorption," and so forth:
this refers to emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) into a contaminated or pure meditative absorption;
for one first enters the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and subsequently enters the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Regarding the clear sequential attainment of the untainted state:
one enters either the sphere of nothingness,
or the sphere of consciousness, or the sphere of infinite space.
Because it is an outflow-free (anāsrava) manifestation, it is said that the final one does not enter this outflow-free concentration through successive meditative attainments (dhyāna);
rather, this concentration arises at the time of penetrating the realm of signless suchness (animitta-tathatā).
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, there is the meditative concentration with signs, up to and including the knowledge that one is emerging from concentration":
this refers to the meditative concentration with signs of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
which enters, abides in, and emerges from concentration by means of the attention with signs (*sanimitta-manasikāra*) involving conceptualization.
If there were no non-conceptual wisdom, one would enter and abide in the state of non-conceptual absorption through the mental attention of non-conceptuality;
it should be known that emergence occurs within a mind characterized by conceptualization of signs.
Jizang says:
"Because of the six kinds of tranquility" refers to the three periods of the mind emerging from seclusion (viveka-citta) below,
and the three periods of the mind being near to emergence (upaniṣad-citta) through tranquility.

Regarding the statement, "Because of the subsiding of the purified consciousness into equanimity, and not because of the equanimity of its support," this explains the predominant function within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
That is to say, in the attainment of cessation, it is merely the purified, untainted consciousness that subsides into equanimity.
It is not by means of prior preparatory effort that there is a mind-concentration;
rather, it is called the "attainment of cessation" because it is equal to the body upon which the attainment of cessation relies.
Regarding the three types of activity and non-activity: if one emerges from the attainment, one first gives rise to mental activity.
Next, bodily activity arises, followed by vocal activity.
Now, it is certainly not the case that there is no such distinction; within the meditative absorption with mind, there exist bodily activities and so forth.
This is the third [explanation] from the *Dharmapada-hetupratyaya-sūtra*.
Within this, first the sūtra to be explained is indicated;
next, it is formally explained.
Within the former, the sūtra text is first cited in its entirety.
The *Pūskā* states:
When a bhikṣu skilled in the Three Piṭakas, or an upāsaka, wishes to inquire based on their understanding, they should do so by means of the eight modes of questioning.
Taiyun says:
"Regarding the Abhidharma-vinaya, one has not yet entered the other two.
Next, the Master of the Treatise provides an explanation.
First, the eight characteristics are enumerated;
subsequently, they are explained individually in sequence.
Initially, it clarifies that "understanding" refers to understanding the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Second, regarding the objects to be remedied by understanding, there are two.
First, because of the defilement of craving for household life,
one does not take delight in the cessation of future existence.
Because of the defilement of views held by the various non-Buddhists, they do not realize [the fruit] despite their aspiration.
The fruit of the threefold comprehension is the abandonment of the two types of defilement: craving and views.
Fourth is the thorough understanding of their intrinsic nature.
Regarding the statement that the three aggregates are established because they serve as the antidotes to the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*):
these are the three aggregates known by the names of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
That is to say, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), which counteracts misconduct;
right mindfulness and right concentration are collectively termed the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), which counteracts all sensual desires;
and right view, right thought, and right effort are collectively termed the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), which counteracts all [wrong] views.
Regarding the fifth, the differentiation of the fruit of realization (*parijñā-phala*):
this refers to that which is comprised within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) resulting from the abandonment and cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The preceding [section] distinguished the fruit of realization by way of its predominance (*adhipati*).
Now, regarding the distinction of the fruits by way of dissociation (*visamyoga*), another explanation is provided:
the former was based on intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while the latter is based on differentiation (*viśeṣa*).

Regarding the six bases for comprehension (*parijñā*), it is further stated that there are four kinds. Jing (Jing) and Buque explain: "First, 'by way of lineage' (*gotra*) refers to the seeds of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); these are the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*)."
Second, by way of its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is the essential nature of concentration (*samādhi*).
Third, by way of its object (*ālambana*), it is the objective sphere of concentration.
Fourth, by way of its accomplishment and so forth, it refers to the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It is only by relying on the two preceding conditions that [the practice] can be accomplished.
Master Ji states:
"The causes and conditions for accomplishment refer precisely to the causes and conditions for attaining meditative concentration."
The remaining three are identical in their significance;
they also state that these are certainly the causes and conditions for accomplishing all meritorious virtues. Ce says:
First, the causal conditions;
second, the essential nature and characteristics of meditative absorption;
third, the conditions for emerging from concentration.
Fourth, the accomplishment of supreme qualities such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*);
seventh, the quality of thorough understanding,
which is further divided into five types.
First, "the cessation of phenomena" refers to the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is because the functional capacity of the seeds of the mind of aversion—which are dissociated from consciousness—constitutes the essence of the cessation of phenomena.
Second, "because it resembles the image of tranquility."
Master Ji said:
"One should know that it is certainly a conventional existence and not an entity with real existence,
for it is merely a similar reflection."
Another interpretation is that this concentration intends to enter into nirvana,
which is the truly quiescent dharma.
Concentration resembles nirvāṇa;
it is an image of tranquility.
Thus, although this cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called an "image" because it resembles nirvāṇa.
There is an interpretation that it is called a "similar image" because it resembles the mind as a shadow does;
regarding the causes and conditions for entering and emerging from the third and fourth [dhyānas],
one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) due to the fear of threats to life.
Because there is no intention to cause harm through that power of concentration;
or because one emerges from meditative absorption for matters such as food, drink, defecation, urination, various illnesses, or bodily excretions;
fifth, for the sake of the merits of emerging from meditative absorption.
This refers to the merits arising at the time of emerging from meditative absorption,
namely, the physical and mental well-being and freedom from all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
If one bestows these upon others, they shall immediately receive the retribution.
The eighth is "thorough understanding and realization. Buque states:
"The Four Truths are called 'realization' (*prāpti*)."
This has already been clarified in the preceding discussion;
it refers to the seven types of wholesome dharmas within the *Vibhāṣā*.
It further emphasizes that the accumulation of observation means that karma is the accumulation of feeling (*vedanā*).
By adding this one type, there are eight.
Regarding the observation of intrinsic nature, one observes the suffering inherent in the essence of sensation (*vedanā*).

Regarding the observation of the causes and conditions for its manifestation in the present life, this refers to its transformation into the origin of sensation, which is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding the observation of the causes and conditions for the cessation of the present turning: this is the observation of the cessation of feeling (*vedanā*).
Regarding the observation of the causes and conditions for the turning of the future: one observes karma as the accumulation of future feeling.
Both the "turning" (*vartana*) and "karma" (*karman*) are capable of producing feeling, and are thus termed the "causes and conditions for turning."
Regarding the observation of the causes and conditions for the cessation of those two [types of] turning:
the Truth of the Path is able to extinguish the two preceding types of observation.
As for the cause and condition for the turning of the cause and condition, it is the observation of the gratification of sensation and craving.
Furthermore, it acts as the causal condition for the transformation of karma;
therefore, it is called the "causal condition of the causal condition of transformation.
As for observing the causal condition of returning, this is likewise the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
Previously, it was stated that the Truth of Cessation functions through transformation and that karma takes cessation as its cause.
Now, one again contemplates feeling as a fault;
this is able to extinguish craving for its flavor, aids the Path, and reveals cessation.
This is called "observing the causes and conditions" and "observing the return," which refers to the repeated observation of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The phrase "accompanied by joy" and so forth is also cited from the sūtra to provide an explanation.
"Counteracting that which is accompanied by pleasure" refers to the citation of the sutra.
"Regarding the most excellent fundamental dhyāna" explains that one relies on the third dhyāna to give rise to the counteractive measure, which is called the practice of the path of pleasure.
When one cultivates and gives rise to insight based on the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) below,
it is called the "path of suffering" because the function of balancing concentration and wisdom is thereby manifested.
The antidote arising from the fourth dhyāna is called "neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

The statement that this is intended to show that [everything] reaches the state of being entirely suffering is for the purpose of causing the attachment to the flavor of feeling and its karmic causes and conditions to be completely severed and extinguished.
Regarding the Buddha’s statement that all feelings are suffering, which is said because those three types of feeling are, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all suffering:
they are all *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of conditioned formations). That this *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* constitutes the underlying principle is what is meant by "ultimate truth."
The phrase "mutual relation" (*pratītya*) refers to the citation of the sutra.
That is to say, "because this exists, that is designated"— this means that pleasure is spoken of in dependence on suffering,
joy is spoken of in dependence on sorrow, and the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*) are thus designated.
However, because everything is suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), it is said here that these various feelings are mutually related,
as they are all subsumed under suffering. Furthermore, it is on account of this ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*) that the designation "one who lacks wisdom" is established.
The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is known only by the noble ones (*ārya*).
That ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not understand it is called "lack of wisdom" (*ajñāna*).
Because this exists, there is established the supramundane wisdom that serves as its antidote.
Because there exists such suffering as the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and its causes,
the supramundane wisdom that remedies them is established;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* says:
For example, a single eyelash on the palm of one's hand goes unnoticed;
yet if it falls into the eye, it causes injury and distress.
Ordinary beings are like the palm of the hand, failing to perceive the eyelash of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
The Noble Ones, like the pupil of the eye, give rise to revulsion and fear because of this;
and it is because of its existence that its result— tranquil nirvāṇa— is established,
namely through the existence of the truths of suffering, origin, and the path.
The designation "the cessation, tranquility,
and nirvāṇa of those" is made because various phenomena are taught as being in mutual opposition to their respective antidotes; nevertheless,
it is by way of such opposition that the existence of various feelings is established.
According to the primary truth (*paramārtha*), all are the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Jì states that the contemplation of the eight aspects is as found at the end of the eighth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
This is also as explained at the end of the fifty-third [fascicle].
Here, the term "relative" refers to designating pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) in contrast to painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*);
it does not mean that pleasant feeling is not suffering.
There are three pairs of correspondences here,
as explained in [text] 56; one should verify them by comparing these pairs.
It is called the *Middha-vinodana-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Dispelling Sleep). Ji says:
It is called a "sleep sūtra" because it explains entering meditative absorption by means of sleep.
There is an explanation:
because it distinguishes the attainment of concentration through the removal of drowsiness, it is called the "Sūtra on Drowsiness.
As for the five kinds of characteristics of the remedies:
1. Being far removed from the signs of darkness;
2. Reaching the principle of preparatory application;
3. Destroying all views.
The fourth is the function of all views;
the fifth is the function of the basis of all views.
First, one cultivates the light that is free from darkness.
Second is the application of exertion through correct initiation.
Regarding the statement "dharmas conducive to uplifting and joy":
the sign of darkness is conducive to sinking, while joy is conducive to uplifting.
Therefore, one initiates the application of effort toward the Dharma of joy;
third, one diminishes various views so that the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the like do not arise;
fourth, one applies effort toward [correct] view.
This refers to that which can produce unwholesome conduct and the sixty-two views and so forth;
it is now being remedied.
The fifth [remedy], which diminishes the seeds of all views, is called "diminishing the basis."
Regarding the five kinds of dharmas that sustain meditative concentration,
Master Ji states:
the first is seclusion.
This is the place of seclusion for meditative concentration.
Second, the place of seclusion refers to the locus for practicing concentration and the teachings conducive to concentration.
Third, the requisites for a mind free from defilement.
That is, regarding the bedding and requisites at the limit.
Fourth, from "from one who possesses wisdom" downwards;
fifth, from "regarding all worlds" downwards.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that the various forms of seclusion, with the state of seclusion as primary,
accord with the two lower types of non-defiled minds.
From "possessing wisdom" downwards there are three;
regarding the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), there are four below [the previous], and within the fifth [category] it is divided into two,
because untainted action (*anāsrava-karman*) constitutes the fifth.
Now it is further explained:
first, remoteness;
second, location.
Third is that which accords with verbal expression;
fourth is that which accords with the requisites for a mind free from defilement;
and fifth, starting from "from one who possesses wisdom" and continuing down to "proper mental attention."
From here below, the third section provides a detailed analysis of the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*) by means of six gates.
First, it clarifies that there are three causes and conditions for being far removed from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*):
first, being far removed from the objects of thought.
Second, the nature of the investigation and analysis of aversion;
third, because one first gives rise to aversion and now correctly distances oneself from it,
it is called the nature of distancing.
The faculty of discursive thought is abandoned through three causes and conditions:
first, those of superior faculties abandon it instantaneously;
second, those of middling faculties abandon it gradually.
Third, those of inferior faculties deeply perceive the faults and afflictions inherent in discursive thought (*vitarka*).

This applies to those concentrations that are either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or pure (*śuddha*).
The two types, vitarka and vicāra, coexist with the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
Whenever one attains any spiritual quality through preliminary application (prayoga), vitarka and vicāra are present;
however, once the fundamental state (maula) is reached, they are no longer present.
If within the eightfold path with outflows (*sāsrava*),
the substance of vitarka is established as right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*); however,
within the branches of the eightfold path without outflows (*anāsrava*), [it is not so].
If it is associated with subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), then right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is established within vitarka and vicāra,
because it gives rise to verbal expression.
Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is simultaneously [associated with] the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*).
In terms of the meaning of the single essence of wisdom, it is spoken of as two:
because it is free from wrong view, it is called right view;
because it is free from wrong thought, it is called right thought.
Because the wisdom of direct realization (sākṣātkāra-jñāna) is not discursive speech,
one cannot establish "right reflection" (samyak-saṃkalpa) by searching for its substance therein. How,
then, is it known that the subsequent wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) arises as speech and is associated with vitarka?
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* asks: "How is it that those with purified awakening [remain] within the defiled meditative absorptions?
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-eight, states:
"In the first defiled absorption, there is no joy and bliss born of separation."
Because it does not arise apart from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the second [dhyāna] with defilement (*sāsrava*), there is no internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*),
because it is agitated and turbid by those afflictions.
In the third defiled [dhyāna], there is no right mindfulness or wisdom,
because it is deluded by superior pleasure.
In the fourth defiled [dhyāna], there is no equanimity or purity of mindfulness.
Because they are defiled by afflictions, this [case] may also be so;
thus, the fifth category is established by excluding those in the formless realms who dwell at the extremes.
Question: Why are the various limit-attainments (*antagrāha*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) not established as factors (*aṅga*)?
Answer: The dhyānas included among the factors are the path of bliss;
the various limit-attainments and formless attainments are the path of suffering.
Therefore, they are not established as [separate] factors.
The *Kṣudraka-śāstra* says: "Because they are all difficult to obtain, one should know that this is said to be suffering.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:

It is only because the fundamental meditative absorption (mauladhyāna) possesses a balance of concentration and wisdom that the Abhidharma treatises do not establish the factors of enlightenment within the formless attainments (ārūpya).
Because this śamatha is of a single flavor,
it constitutes the sixth benefit of the antidote.
Those two rely upon three types of establishments.
Question: Why is it that in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are the antidote and joy and bliss are the benefit,
whereas in the second dhyāna, only internal purity is mentioned as the antidote?
Joy and bliss constitute the benefit.
In the third dhyāna, there are three factors— establishment of mindfulness, equanimity, and correct wisdom—
which serve as the remedy for bliss and thus constitute the benefit.
In the fourth dhyāna, pure mindfulness and equanimity are established;
these serve as antidotes to neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation and for the sake of benefit, and so forth,
as they all belong to the same level of dhyāna.
Why is it that the benefits of the remedies differ in degree?
Answer: The first dhyāna remedies the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the desire realm, unwholesome states (*adharma*) are most numerous.
Therefore, the two factors of vitarka and vicāra must be applied as remedies.
Because one has newly departed from distraction at the beginning, joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha) are established as benefits.
Since the faults in the first dhyāna are few, the single factor of internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) is established within the second dhyāna as a remedy.
Because it first abandons the afflictions of the meditative state,
joy and bliss are established as its benefits;
in the third dhyāna, however, there are various obstacles belonging to that very stage.
Therefore, three remedies are established:
mindfulness and equanimity are established to prevent the joy of the lower stages,
and right knowledge is established to prevent the pleasure of one's own stage.
Within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), this pleasure is the most supreme;
therefore, one branch is established as pleasure for the sake of benefit.
Regarding yoga, some say it consists of mindfulness, equanimity, and correct knowledge (*samyak-jñāna*).
It serves only to guard against the joy of the lower stages.
Within the fourth dhyāna, there is only the obstacle of another stage—
namely, the pleasure of the third dhyāna— and thus mindfulness and equanimity are established as the antidote.
Since the transformation of suffering and pleasure has been ultimately transcended,
only that which is neither painful nor pleasant is established as beneficial bliss. Thus,
the seventh dhyāna factor is established or discarded through a comparative analysis of its penetration and obstruction within the categories of the path-factors (*mārga-aṅga*).
Thus, regarding these two dharmas, there are similarities and differences in the way their essential natures and characteristics interpenetrate.
For this reason, in the treatise, one first establishes four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to determine the relative breadth and narrowness of the two dharmas;
subsequently, based on these four propositions, one clarifies their respective abolition and establishment.
The factors of dhyāna (dhyānāṅga) are eighteen in name, but ten in substance. These are:
vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, cittaikāgratā, adhyātmasaṃprasāda, smṛti, upekṣā, saṃprajanya, and aduḥkhāsukha.
The factors of the path (mārga-pakṣya-dharma) are thirty-seven in name,
but their substance consists of only ten:
namely, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, tranquility, equanimity, volition, and ethical discipline.
Among these, there are three factors that are members of dhyāna but not members of the path:
namely, vicāra, sukha, and aduḥkhāsukha.
There are four factors that are members of the path but not members of dhyāna.
There are six factors that are both limbs of dhyāna and limbs of the path: namely,
vitarka, prīti, ekāgratā, smṛti, upekṣā, and saṃprajanya.
That which is neither [of the two] excludes what has been stated above.
Having thus identified the validity or invalidity of the four propositions, the following section distinguishes between their rejection and establishment.

Question: Regarding vicāra (investigation), sukha (pleasure), and aduḥkhāsukha (neither-pain-nor-pleasure), why are they established only as factors of dhyāna (meditative absorption) and not as factors of the mārga (path)?
Explanation: It is said that...
Right view is the constituent body of the path;
those factors that accord with that path are established as limbs of the path.
Those three, such as vitarka and so forth, do not accord with the path.
Therefore, the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are not established [therein]. What is inconsistent about this?
The commentary says:
Investigation is overshadowed by the force of applied thought;
pleasure is overshadowed by pliancy;
and neither-pain-nor-pleasure is overshadowed by equanimity of formation.
Therefore, the factors of dhyāna (dhyānāṅga) are established, but the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are not.
Question: For what reason are the four—faith, exertion, pliancy, and ethical discipline—not established as factors of dhyāna?
Answer: The factors of dhyāna are based on having already entered [the state of] the Dharma.
Faith is the primary gateway for entering the Dharma;
therefore, among the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga), faith is not established as a factor of dhyāna. The factors of dhyāna pertain to abiding in accordance with the meditative state.
Because it is incited by diligence (*vīrya*), it does not abide in accordance [with the mind];
therefore, it is included among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) rather than among the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*).
Furthermore, while the factors of dhyāna constitute the path of bliss, diligence is incited by exertion; thus, it is characterized by hardship rather than bliss.
Therefore, among the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), it does not conform to the factors of dhyāna. Lightness and tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) are included among the factors of the path;
because one is freed from evil, body and mind come to rest, and thus lightness and tranquility are established.
In the dhyānas, the experience of pleasure (sukha-vedanā) obscures that pliancy (praśrabdhi);
therefore, pliancy is not established [as a separate factor].
Question: Why is ethical discipline (śīla) included among the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga), whereas it is not established as a branch of dhyāna?
The commentary states:
Because the associated [factors] have the sense of possessing power and function when taking an object as their condition,
the factors of dhyāna are established.
The essence of the precepts does not stand without conditions;
the factors of dhyāna alone do not suffice. However, within the Eightfold Noble Path, the wheel of the Middle Way serves as the hub;
therefore, the path-factors are established.
Next, the following is an explanation according to the text.
Regarding the statement that "inner serenity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and equanimity constitute its intrinsic nature," this means that in the two meditative absorptions (dhyānas),
mindfulness, clear comprehension, and equanimity do not take external objects as their focal point.
Within the internal door, being free from sinking and floating,
the purification of the mind through the equality of the three factors is called "internal serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).
Regarding the fourth dhyāna, both equanimity (upekṣā) and mindfulness (smṛti) are said to be "pure."
Because it is free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the four types of feeling, inhalation and exhalation,
and the eight higher afflictions, it is called "pure.
It is said that the second dhyāna possesses functional activity by virtue of its own nature.
In the second dhyāna, there are equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension;
these truly perform the function of removing applied and sustained thought.
Nevertheless, because it is disturbed by the secondary affliction of mental agitation characteristic of that stage, it is collectively designated by the name "internal serenity."
Regarding the statement that the third dhyāna is "already free from" [joy] to reveal its intrinsic nature:
the third concentration is free from the secondary affliction associated with joy;
it reveals that its intrinsic nature consists of the triad of mindfulness, wisdom, and equanimity.
The fourth section clarifies the establishment [of the factors].
First, a question is posed.

The intent of the question is as follows: what is the purpose of establishing these four or five factors within the four dhyānas? Regardless of other considerations, the intent is to clarify that within each respective dhyāna, these factors are established for the sake of providing remedies and benefits.
Because those two rely on the three meanings of samādhi,
four or five factors are accordingly established.
Within this passage, there are six successive expositions.
Regarding the initial statement "the basis of abiding" and so forth,
this refers to what the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* describes as the antidotes, benefits, and bliss.
As for "abiding," it is called abiding because one remains fixedly upon a single object through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because the factors of counteraction can sever the hindrances to concentration,
causing concentration to arise and serving as its basis,
they are called "benefactors that provide a basis for abiding."
This is the factor of benefit (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*).
To have joy and bliss within and to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in its full perfection is called "beneficial.
Its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the substance of that concentration.
This refers to the two types of samādhi as their basis.
Second, regarding the subsequent section:
what is meant by "contemplating the object of focus"?
Contemplating the obstacles to be remedied and thereby generating weary detachment is the branch of the antidote.
As for "partaking of the object of focus":
Joyful delight in the experience of objects is the limb of benefit;
it consists in not being distracted by those objects.
This is one branch of the mind.
Thirdly, as for what is meant by "the basis of benefit":
Because it serves as the basis for counteracting obstacles, it benefits meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the basis of the higher mental states (*adhicitta*),
this refers to joy, bliss, and so forth, which serve as the basis for superior concentration.
Regarding that which is the basis for superior wisdom:
meditative concentration is the basis for wisdom;
this means that the former serves as the basis for the latter.
Fourthly, in order to counteract the three types of dwelling in defilement (*saṃkleśa-vihāra*),
there is first the dwelling in affliction (*kliṣṭa-vihāra*).
That which is eliminated by the factors of counteraction (*pratipakṣāṅga*) is the dwelling in suffering and affliction;
that which is eliminated by the factors of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*) is [the opposite].
Regarding the third, abiding in delusion:
through the wisdom arising from meditative concentration (samādhi), one abandons that delusion.
This is the fifth section.
To distinguish them by means of an analogy:
those who are actively seeking wealth are likened to the branch of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa-aṅga*);
those who are properly enjoying it are likened to the branch of benefit (*anuśaṃsa-aṅga*).
Regarding that mastery, it is like a branch of one-pointedness.
In the sixth section,
as for the establishment of the branches of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to counteract self-inflicted asceticism:
This means that ascetic practices and afflictions can cause the Noble Path to diminish;
thus, these afflictions are termed "obstructions to the diminution of the remedy.
Since vitarka and vicāra can counteract these [afflictions], they are called the "remedies for the obstructions to the diminution of the remedy."
Joy and bliss are the antidotes to the affliction of body and mind;
one-pointedness of mind is the antidote to the scattering [of the mind] toward external objects.
Regarding the fifth [topic], the explanation of seclusion, a question is first posed.
Why is it that in the Sūtra, regarding the first dhyāna, after stating "freedom from desire," it further states "distancing oneself from evil and unwholesome dharmas"?
Answer: There are five successive explanations.
First, freedom from the specific characteristics of the five sensual desires is termed "freedom from desire."
Abstaining from misconduct is called "abstaining from the unwholesome.
The second [category] is the abandonment of the desire for afflictions;
it is distinguished from the former by the abandonment of karmic defilements.

The third [stage] abandons the desire for the objects of enjoyment used by householders, as well as the three types of evil vitarka-vicāra (discursive thoughts) of those who have left the home life, thereby distinguishing it from the other two.
The fourth abandons the *kāma-vitarka* (thoughts of sensual desire) and the *vyāpāda-vitarka* (thoughts of ill will), thereby distinguishing it from the other two. Fifth, furthermore, Zhongjing says:
This is also the same as what the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say: having departed from those [states], one performs incantations and the like;
this is called "departing from evil and unwholesomeness. Tai says:
Non-Buddhists are initially able to abandon desire and attain the marks of the five supernormal powers;
furthermore, it is shown that even after they have fallen from those states, they perform incantations and curses—
this is called "being free from evil and unwholesome dharmas."
The sixth [section] explains the gateway to suffering.
First, it asks:
according to principle, sorrow and suffering exist only in the desire realm, as they have already been severed in the first dhyāna.
How is it known that suffering exists in the first dhyāna and is only severed in the second?
In the passage providing the answer below, Jing says:
"Although the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) is absent, there still remains the coarseness of suffering (*duḥkha-dausthulya*)."
Dauṣṭhulya is the state of being unrefined, the lack of flexibility, and the lack of tranquility within the faculty of suffering;
it is only in the second dhyāna that this is severed,
just as when an abscess is lanced and the pus and blood are completely drained.
Within that body, there still exists a state of unease and lack of pliancy called *dauṣṭhulya*.
Next, a counter-objection is raised:
if the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has already been severed in the first dhyāna, [how can this be so?]
It is indistinguishable from its correspondence with the second dhyāna;
therefore, it is concluded below. Tai says:
Because joy (*prīti*) is not yet fulfilled within the first dhyāna, the seeds of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) exist;
in the other dhyānas, the lack of flexibility in those seeds is termed the "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to that category.
Because the state of coarse dysfunction (*dausthulya*) induced by this faculty of suffering has not yet been extinguished,
it is not said that the faculty of suffering is severed in the first dhyāna;
furthermore, when entering the second absorption, one is fully satisfied with joy (*prīti*).
All seeds are thoroughly satisfied;
because there is no lack of pliancy induced by the faculty of suffering,
it is said that the two meditative attainments extinguish the faculty of suffering.
If one considers the seeds of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),
even those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) do not sever the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of that faculty of suffering;
it is just as when black iron enters fire and becomes red, yet upon being removed from the fire, it returns to blackness and the red color vanishes.
Therefore, its suffering and its gross heaviness are likewise so.
When entering the two higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), joy is extinguished and equanimity increases;
when emerging from the two higher absorptions and entering the first absorption, equanimity is again extinguished and joy arises.
Master Ji said:
"The 'coarse and heavy' (dauṣṭhulya) refers to the unserviceability (akarmanyatā) that follows its respective basis;
however, because the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna still possess joy (prīti), they are not yet fully perfected."
Because the coarse and heavy [defilements] have not yet been exhausted,
and because the three consciousnesses accord with the faculty of suffering,
whereas joy is directly opposed to the faculty of suffering.

This refers to the abandonment of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*), outflows (*āsrava*), and the nature of dependence (*āśrayatva*) associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) by one who has abandoned [the afflictions];
it does not mean the abandonment of the seeds or their association with consciousness, because these have already been abandoned previously.
As for the unwholesome seeds:
It may be said that the first dhyāna has already been abandoned because it co-exists with consciousness;
however, if it is wholesome or indeterminate,
even an Arhat still gives rise to it.
If there is the contaminated second dhyāna,
it suppresses the suffering and heaviness of the contaminated;
if there is the uncontaminated second dhyāna, it abandons the heaviness and the uncontaminated joy.
Those who are not non-retrogressive do not possess this.
Entering the first dhyāna, coarse and heavy states arise;
this is the seventh gate of dissolution and movement.
It is as has been stated: these vitarka and vicāra exist within the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*).

Therefore, the treatise asks: "If vitarka, vicāra, and so forth are all able to assist and benefit the superior samādhi of the first dhyāna, and can also sustain the dhyānas of their own stage, making them pure, for what reason did the Blessed One say they are called 'agitation' (*iñjita*)?"
However, according to the tradition of the West, vitarka and vicāra exist only within the stage of the preparatory application (prayoga-bhūmi).
Eighth, the explanation of the superior factors:
The question asks why the four factors of the second dhyāna are superior to the five factors of the first dhyāna.
Up to the fourth [dhyāna], which has four factors, is it superior to the third, which has five?
Answer: There are three reasons.
First, the relationship between the object of abandonment and its antidote.
In the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra serve as the antidotes,
while sensual desires and evil states are the objects to be countered.
In the second dhyāna, internal serenity serves as the antidote.
Vitarka and vicāra are the factors to be remedied.
In the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension serve as the remedies for the factors to be remedied, such as joy;
therefore, one knows it to be superior.
In the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra serve as the antidote;
with respect to the second dhyāna, they are the objects to be remedied.
This continues up to the third dhyāna, where bliss serves as the benefit.
The fourth dhyāna is regarded as that which is to be remedied;
by this, one knows that what is above is superior and what is below is inferior.
This is the attainment of the superior benefit.
The benefits of the various stages likewise range from superior to inferior;
as for that which is realized,
the essence of the one mind also ranges from inferior to superior.
Regarding the statement that [the factors] are subsumed under five branches according to their respective applications:
it is called "five branches" because the mention of the many includes the few.
In the ninth section, the "Gate of Explaining the Distinctions," it is stated that the second dhyāna excels the first in terms of the perfection of its essential nature;
the third, however, excels the second in terms of the fulfillment of its branches of benefit.
The fourth [section] is superior to the third because it concerns purity through detachment from defilements.
Thus concludes the first four of the five major sections of the "Decisive Investigation of the Stage of Meditative Equipoise" (samāhitabhūmi) presented above.
From here below is the fifth section, which provides a comprehensive explanation through six gates.
First, it clarifies the four types of meditative cultivation;
it begins by stating their number and listing their names.
This is subsequently established by way of persons.
Within this, first the four types of cultivation of concentration based on four types of persons are explained;
subsequently, these are further analyzed in response to specific difficulties.
Master Jing and others have said:
"The four treatises on the cultivation of meditative concentration all clarify this;
however, in distinguishing what is cultivated, there are not insignificant differences."
In this present text, four types of practitioners are further cited to distinguish four modes of cultivation;
there is no mention of these elsewhere,
for they exist only in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Regarding those who have already seen the truths through the "swift penetration" of the first suffering:
these individuals of sharp faculties do not further seek to become sharper,
yet they have not yet attained the fundamental present bliss.
Relying on future-dhyāna, one attains the first two [stages] definitively;
however, seeking only the present bliss of the fundamental dhyāna, one practices concentration.
If one is of dull faculties yet craves superior faculties, [one should practice accordingly].
Because they do not seek that fundamental happiness of the present life,
it is not mentioned. Second,
there are ordinary beings who have not yet attained the path, as well as those sentient beings who have already attained the immeasurables and are free from desire.
Although this person may seek the happiness of the present life,
they instead desire to seek a place of rebirth in the future;
therefore, they cultivate the divine eye to see future events.
Therefore, it is taught selectively.
For those who have attained the path of practice through the slow penetration of the three joys and have already seen the truths,
as well as for Arhats of dull faculties whose various tasks are already fulfilled.
Those who cultivate the third type of wisdom, the analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāna-prajñā*), solely for the purpose of transforming their faculties,
are those who have attained the fourfold swift penetration of joy through hearing,
reflection, cultivation, and realization; they are those who have already established the path and seen the truths.
This person of sharp faculties,
being an Anāgāmin who has already attained the fundamental four dhyānas and has nothing further to accomplish,
seeks only the fruit of Arhatship through the exhaustion of outflows.
The following objections will be examined in detail.
Among the four types of persons, the first and the last are easy to understand, while the middle two are somewhat difficult; therefore, the author of the treatise examines them in detail.
In this context, up until the purification of knowledge and vision,
this ordinary person has already suppressed the afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation and attained the fundamental dhyānas for the bliss of the present life.
One cultivates the four immeasurables and the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñāna-abhijñā*),
because one universally observes the future.
It is said that if one has already realized this supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death, it is called "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*).
Regarding the statement, "If one delights in the practice of slow progress, when the path proceeds until right knowledge arises," Jing says:
This clarifies that an Arhat who seeks to transform their faculties cultivates the concentration of analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāna-prajñā-samādhi*).
At that time, vitarka, vicāra, vedanā, and saṃjñā give rise to craving and views;
with craving and views as the root,
they initiate karma and produce rebirth.
One contemplates suffering and its origin;
seeking liberation from them, one contemplates cessation.
In this manner, one repeatedly gives rise to the wisdom born of hearing and cultivates the wisdom of analytical discernment.
Having further sharpened one's faculties, one repeatedly contemplates the Four Noble Truths;
cultivating discerning wisdom and abiding in right mindfulness constitutes the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).
One should give rise to right knowledge, which is liberation.
When an Aśaikṣa transforms their faculties, there are nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation;
only then does it become transformed into the sharp [faculties].
This statement is made based on the Hīnayāna perspective. Tái says:
"It is because of dull faculties."

Furthermore, the desire for dharmas that give rise to wholesome roots within the desire realm—such as sensation (*saṃjñā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), discursive thought (*vitarka*), and the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*)—is called the "discriminating wisdom of the faculty" (*indriya-vibhāga-prajñā*).
Jì (Jizang) says: [omitted].
Because of this dull faculty,
one dwells with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, discerning through wisdom regarding the wholesome phenomena of the desire realm— namely, sensation, perception, and applied thought.
This refers to those who seek sharp faculties yet fear falling back from their practice.
"Feeling" (vedanā) signifies the meaning of repeatedly experiencing and receiving;
it refers to the increased experience of the pleasures of desire and so forth.
This refers to the objective spheres of all phenomena that take up mental images.
"Investigation" (*vitarka*) refers to the co-occurrence of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), as well as applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Within this context, one gives rise to right mindfulness because, through the transformation of perception, mindfulness would otherwise be lost.
When right mindfulness arises, one generates discerning wisdom.
Second, regarding the clarity of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and the departure from desire, there are six types;
as in the sixth chapter of the Abhidharma, there are ten kinds.
The opening and closing differ.
Third, the explanation of the four synonyms for dhyāna:
Why is it called *samādhi* (concentration), and so forth, up to "because it sustains the mind"?
Tài says: *Brahma-svara-samādhi* is here translated as *samāhita*.

When the objects manifested by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) are similar in their preceding and succeeding moments, they are designated as "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) because they are alike.
The object of focus known by the concentrated mind is the basis of that concentration;
from the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the concentrated mind, all reflected images arise as objects.
When focusing upon these objects, one remains free from sinking and agitation, abiding in equanimity and maintaining stability.
The mind abiding on a single object is called *samādhi*.
Jing says: "In meditative concentration, the mental image (*pratibimba*) that serves as the focal object resembles its original substrate (*bimba*)."
This is called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
Fourth, it is clarified that there are ten conditions for falling away.
As for Aśvajit, the old *Abhidharmakośa* states that he was the bhikṣu Kṛṣṇadanta, whose name was Ālu.
In truth, one should say "Aśva," which here means "horse";
"vada" means "superior."
He was a bhikṣu who debated with the Brahmā King.
Because he received honor and sustenance, he fell away like Devadatta.
Since Devadatta possessed sharp faculties, why did he fall away?
Tài said: "One who manifests [sharp] conduct is not necessarily sharp, and one who manifests [dull] conduct is not necessarily dull.

Tai said: "As for what is called 'unshared ignorance' (āveṇika-avidyā)..."
The commentary by Rakṣācandra states:
Because the six consciousnesses clearly perceive external objects,
the clarity of views, craving, and so forth becomes correspondingly strong.
The power of ignorance is weak and arises following views and craving;
it possesses associated ignorance.
The manas internally takes as its object an indistinct realm.
The power of ignorance is strong, while that of views, craving, and pride is weak;
because the functional efficacy of ignorance surpasses that of the other three afflictions,
it is called "unshared" (āveṇika).
To speak according to the actual principle,
views, craving, pride, and so forth should be termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*);
however, within the system of the Hīnayāna, two types of ignorance— the associated and the non-associated— are established.
Therefore, among ignorance (*avidyā*), it is described as "unshared" (*āveṇika*);
among views (*dṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and pride (*māna*), the term "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) is not mentioned.
Master Śīlabhadra explains: [text continues]
The ignorance of the manas and the mind of the three natures [are unique];

In the commentary, it is explained by citing the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
It is called "unique" because these are not shared with the two vehicles; likewise, the ignorance of the six consciousnesses is not shared with the ignorance of the manas.
One should receive the name "unshared" (āveṇika).
The eighteen unshared dharmas are not shared with the two vehicles;
nevertheless, they function in conjunction with virtues of a similar class.
The ignorance of the manas is likewise.
It is called "unshared" (āveṇika) because it does not share its name with the ignorance of the six consciousnesses;
however, it functions in conjunction with its own class of afflictions, such as the latent tendencies of views and craving.
This differs from the Hinayana interpretation, which defines "unshared" (*āveṇika*) as that which does not function in common [with others].
According to the commentary, citing the eighteen unshared dharmas (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikadharma*),
it can only be called "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikāvidyā*).
It would be incorrect to give the name "unshared ignorance" (āveṇikī avidyā) to it alone;
since the views, craving, pride, and so forth of the manas are likewise not shared with the six consciousnesses,
they too should be called "unshared."
Nor is this contradictory,
